newsitem.title: UK: Britain urges N.Irish Protestants to keep truce.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges N.Irish Protestants to keep truce.

text.p: Britain urged Northern Irish Protestant guerrillas on Tuesday to hold to their shaky two-year-old ceasefire and avert a return to sectarian strife.

"I very much hope that that ceasefire can be maintained," Britain's minister for the province, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said as fears intensified that pro-British Protestant "Loyalists" might end their truce and resume a war against Roman Catholic republican nationalists.
Catholic leaders piled pressure on the guerrilla irish Republican Army, the Loyalists' arch-foes, to call their own ceasefire and defuse tension.
But Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, said it was up to Britain to breathe life into Northern Ireland's faltering peace process.

A leading Protestant politician linked to Loyalist guerrillas said they would "obviously...re-assess the situation" following Monday's announcement by jailed Loyalists they had lost faith in the peace process.
Mayhew gave a warning that any weakening of the Loyalists' truce would play into the hands of the IRA which is fighting to end British rule of the province and unite it with Ireland.
"For it to be abandoned could only serve the interests of the very people to whom Loyalists are very strongly opposed," Mayhew told a Belfast news conference.
The Loyalist prisoners' decision followed a string of IRA bomb attacks in mainland Britain and a foiled bomb attack by republican dissidents in Belfast.
John White, leader of the Protestant Ulster Democratic Party, said sectarian bloodshed could return if the IRA launched more attacks but he believed the truce would hold "at this moment".
"If there is any reaction from Sinn Fein/IRA, then it makes it much more difficult and there is every likelihood that there could be a return to full-scale conflict," said White.
Loyalists answered an IRA truce in September 1994 with their own ceasefire the following October. The IRA ended their truce last February but the Loyalists' shaky ceasefire has continued.
Cardinal Cahal Daly, retiring as spiritual head of the island's five million Roman Catholics, said IRA violence was the chief obstacle to Sinn Fein getting a place at peace talks.
"No single thing would do more at this time to restore hope and lessen division in our society than a reinstatement of the IRA ceasefire," Daly told reporters in Armagh, west of Belfast.

Seamus Mallon, deputy leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, said the Loyalists' statement had created a "serious situation, a potential threat to the peace process". He also called for an IRA ceasefire.
Adams said Britain should learn from the Middle East peace efforts and allow Sin Fein into new negotiations. It is barred from current multi-party talks because the IRA is on a war footing.

"The British government has yet to create the climate or indeed the practicalities for real talks," Adams said. "There were disastrous events in the Middle East... Today in Washington the (rival) leaders are meeting.
"Compare that to what is happening here, when people are being cut out, marginalised, excluded. John Major should take example."
